title: From the heart (Mark 7:1–23)
hook: it's what comes out of the heart that makes unclean

segments.voice: Yesterday, it is I: Jesus on the water, and rowers who weren't alone. Your line was it is I. Where were you rowing hard? Today, an argument about washing hands. Day two hundred ten.

The kitchen gets cleaned when guests are coming. The profile picture gets polished. The right thing gets said at the right moment. The outside is the easy part. Then there's what comes out when nobody's performing. The comment under your breath in traffic. The text you send when you're angry. What you say about someone once they've left the room. In today's reading, an argument about clean hands turns into a teaching about exactly that. Today: from the heart.
screen: `THE CLEAN KITCHEN FOR GUESTS.` → `THE COMMENT UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT HANDS.`

segments.voice: First, the washing. Some Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and notice that some of Jesus's disciples eat bread without washing their hands in the ritual way. Mark stops to explain the custom: the Pharisees, holding the tradition of the elders, washed their hands before eating, and washed cups and pots too. This wasn't about germs. Some scholars explain it as a practice of holiness, bringing something of the Temple's purity to an ordinary table. A ritual handwashing with a blessing before bread is still part of Jewish practice today. Second, the challenge. Jesus answers with the prophet Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." He gives an example: a man who declares his goods corban, a gift set aside for God, and so does nothing for his father or mother. The rule is kept; the parents get nothing. Third, the saying. Then he calls the crowd and says it plainly: "There is nothing from without a man that entering into him, can defile him. But the things which come from a man, those are they that defile a man." Later, alone with the disciples, he explains: "For from within out of the heart of men proceed evil thoughts", and the list goes on: murders, thefts, covetousness, deceit, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride. Fourth, how this is read. Mark adds a short aside here, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "purging all meats"; some translations take it to mean Jesus made all foods clean, and Christians came to eat any food. Observant Jews continue to keep the food laws as God's commandments, and hear this debate as one among teachers. Catholics hear its center in the saying itself: in Mark's telling, what defiles a person starts on the inside.
screen: `A TRADITION OF CLEAN HANDS.` · `LIPS NEAR, HEART FAR.` · `NOTHING FROM WITHOUT CAN DEFILE.` · `WHAT COMES OUT OF THE HEART.` · then, large: `THEIR HEART IS FAR FROM ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch your words. Settle, and breathe. Think back over yesterday. What came out of you? Not what you planned to say, what actually came out. A kind word. A sharp one. Something about someone behind their back. Don't argue with yourself; just look. Then look underneath: what was in your heart when it came out? Tired? Hurt? Afraid? If you pray, you can offer your heart to God as it is, and ask for a clean one. If you don't, just notice. The bell holds the time.
From the heart. Jesus's teaching that what makes a person unclean isn't what goes in, but what comes out of the heart. Today's word.

Your line: out of the heart. This week: Legion sent home, two daughters healed, the carpenter at home, the twelve sent out, rest, the rowers, and now the heart. Today, for one hour, listen to every word you say, and hear where it came from. Day two hundred ten.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this gospel at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the daily examination of conscience, reviewing words and actions and the heart behind them, is a Catholic practice.

original.note: Greek: heart, in the Bible the center of thought, will and feeling, not only emotion.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus didn't care about washing hands.
what it means: holiness isn't only on the outside; what defiles a person comes out of the heart.
what a scholar hears: kardia, the seat of will; Mark's aside at 7:19 that he 'made all foods clean', read differently by Christians and Jews.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 7:6, 7:15 and 7:21 given from memory; confirm.

The Pharisees' handwashing is framed respectfully as a practice of holiness, and the modern Jewish practice (netilat yadayim with its blessing before bread) is noted. A Keeper and a Jewish reader should check the framing.
Mark 7:19 'purging all meats' (Douay) / 'making all foods clean': Christians and Jews read this differently; stated without ranking.
The vice list is abridged from 7:21–22.

Reviewer pass: the Temple-purity explanation of the handwashing is one scholarly reading, now hedged ('many scholars explain'); 'Jews still wash' narrowed to 'many observant Jews'. The parenthetical at 7:19 (Douay 'purging all meats') is read by many modern translations as Mark's comment that Jesus declared all foods clean, but the reading is debated; now hedged as 'many translations read Mark as adding'.

Editor review: hook no longer opens 'Think about' or tells the listener 'most of us'; 'many scholars' and 'many observant Jews' claims softened; corban retold as Mark has it (nothing done for father or mother, no 'aging' or 'hungry'); the vice list now follows the Douay terms; the 7:19 aside is quoted from the Douay ('purging all meats') and no longer attributed to 'many translations'; the narrator's 'God looks at the heart' is now framed as Mark's telling.
